ATS RESUME CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Will your resume even reach a human? Run the copy-paste test.

Most job applications go through an applicant tracking system before anyone reads them, and it extracts your resume's text the same mechanical way copying it out by hand does. Select all the text in your resume file, copy it, and paste it below — this page reads the exact same extraction for the specific, well-documented formatting problems that break it: icon-font bullets that paste as garbage, missing section headings, contact info buried where a parser won't look, and layouts that scramble when flattened to plain text.

Nothing is uploaded. The text you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Copy the text out of your resume file

Open your resume (PDF or Word), select all the text (Ctrl+A / Cmd+A), and copy it (Ctrl+C / Cmd+C). Do not retype it — the whole point is testing what a mechanical extraction produces, not what you meant to write.

2. Paste it here

Paste your resume text above and click Check my resume.

What was found

3. Optional: match it to a job posting

Paste the full text of one job posting. This reads the skills, tools and qualifications the posting leans on and shows which your resume already covers and which it never mentions, most important first. It is a wording check, not a promise of an interview — only add a term if you genuinely have that experience.

Uses the resume text from step 2 and the posting above. Nothing is sent anywhere unless you add an AI key in the wording-changes box below the result.

How your resume covers this posting

Mentioned in the posting, missing from your resume

    Already covered

      The percentage is this page's own weighted coverage of the terms it could read from the posting (repeated, required and title terms count more; "nice to have" terms count less). It is not an applicant tracking system's score. Plain-word and phrase matching cannot tell that two different words mean the same thing unless it knows the pair.

      Suggest wording changes (optional)

      Without a key you get, for each missing term, the line of your resume closest to how the posting uses it, and a plain instruction. With your own key from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a model rewrites up to five of your existing lines. Your resume text and the posting are then sent from this browser to the provider you choose, and nowhere else; the key stays in this tab and is not saved. Suggestions are drafts: keep a change only if it is true.

      What this does and doesn't check

      Steps 1–2 read the text you paste for symptoms that are documented to break ATS text extraction: icon-font characters standing in for bullets, corrupted text, missing standard section headings, missing or buried contact information, missing dates, and signs of a multi-column layout collapsing into one line. Step 3 separately compares your wording with one job posting you paste. It does not check achievement phrasing or grammar — and it cannot see your file's actual visual layout (columns, text boxes, images), only what copied out as text, which is exactly what most parsers see too.

      More on the technique: what the ATS copy-paste test is and why it works. Wondering how the keyword match differs from a paid scanner? See how this checker compares to Jobscan. Wondering if you even need a tool for this? See what an eyeball scan of the pasted text usually misses.

      Common questions

      What is the ATS copy-paste test?

      Copy all the text out of your resume file (Ctrl+A, Ctrl+C from the PDF or Word document — never retype it) and look at what comes out. Applicant tracking systems extract resume text the same mechanical way, so a garbled, out-of-order, or incomplete copy is a strong sign the same content will not parse correctly.

      Does this tell me whether my resume will pass a specific company's ATS?

      No. ATS products differ in how they extract and score text, and this tool has no visibility into any specific employer's system. It reports evidence from the text you pasted — formatting symptoms that are documented to cause parsing problems across most systems — and leaves the decision to you.

      Why paste text instead of uploading my resume file?

      Uploading a file means a server somewhere reads your resume's contents. Pasting text you already copied keeps everything in your browser — nothing about your resume ever leaves your device — and it doubles as the copy-paste test itself: if the paste comes out garbled, that is the finding.

      What if my resume is already text and copies out perfectly?

      Then the format check will likely report no findings, which is a good sign for the checks it runs — but format is only half of it. Step 3 compares your wording with a job posting you paste; it still does not judge achievement phrasing or grammar.

      No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not career, legal, or any other professional advice, and it does not tell you whether any specific employer's applicant tracking system will accept your resume — only whether the text you pasted shows documented signs of a broken format. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

      Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — the text you paste is not saved anywhere by this tool.

      Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded to us; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. The one request this page can make is to the AI provider you choose, when you press Suggest wording changes with your own key: it carries your resume text and the posting, and nothing else. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, match_run, tailor_run) are counted only in local storage on your device and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

      Pricing your own client work rather than applying for a role? The freelance retainer calculator works a sustainable monthly retainer out of your income goal, capacity, overhead, and utilization — nothing uploaded.

      Applying to many roles at once? The job application tracker keeps your list, shows which follow-ups are due and which sources reply, and never uploads it.

      Applying as a musician or band rather than for a role? The EPK generator builds the electronic press kit a venue, festival, or blog will ask for instead of a resume — same job, different gatekeeper.

      Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-it-by-eye.html.text:
← ATS resume checker

ATS Resume Checker vs. eyeballing the copy-paste test yourself

The copy-paste test is a manual technique first, and you do not need this page's tool to run it: copy the text out of your resume file, paste it into a plain editor, and look at what comes out. This checker only automates that same paste through the same fixed set of documented checks, so it is worth being specific about what a quick look tends to miss.

Where an eyeball scan of the pasted text usually falls short

What the same pasted text looks like read by eye vs. checked by rule.
SymptomReading it yourselfThis checker
Icon-font / private-use characters standing in for bulletsOften renders as a tiny blank box or nothing visible, so it reads as ordinary spacing next to your bullet text.Matches the exact Unicode range (U+E000–U+F8FF) regardless of how it renders, and counts every occurrence.
Contact info buried past the top of the documentNothing to look at — you would have to manually find your email and estimate how far into the paste it sits.Measures the exact position of the first email or phone match as a fraction of the document.
Mid-line gaps from a collapsed multi-column layoutFour or five spaces in the middle of a line looks like normal spacing unless you count characters.Flags any line with four or more spaces (or a tab) mid-line, and reports how many lines are affected.
Missing or non-standard section headingsYou know your own resume's structure, so a heading you wrote yourself never looks wrong to you.Checks the pasted text against the specific heading phrasings a parser is documented to look for.
Does anything I paste get uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The check runs entirely in your browser; nothing you paste is sent to a server.

None of this means the manual version is wrong to try first — it is the same technique, and it is free either way. A read-through is genuinely good at catching the paste that comes out almost entirely blank, or one that is visibly scrambled top to bottom. What it is not good at is counting: how many lines have a mid-line gap, what fraction of the document your contact info falls within, or spotting a character that renders as nothing at all. This checker runs the same fixed rules against the same paste every time.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the checker runs in your browser, and it keeps working with the connection off once loaded.

Run the free ATS copy-paste test

Common questions

Can't I just do the copy-paste test myself without this tool?

Yes -- the copy-paste test is a manual technique first, and this checker only automates it. Copy the text out of your resume file, paste it into any plain-text editor, and look at what comes out. That alone catches the most obvious breakage: a paste that is almost entirely blank, or one that is visibly scrambled. What a quick look tends to miss is covered below.

What does an eyeball scan of the pasted text usually miss?

Three things most often. First, icon-font characters (used for decorative bullets or checkmarks in some templates) often render as a tiny invisible box or nothing at all in a plain editor, so their presence is easy to not notice even though an ATS parser sees the same unreadable code point. Second, whether your contact info sits early enough in the extracted text is a position you would have to measure, not something that jumps out visually. Third, four or more spaces in the middle of a line -- the signature of a collapsed multi-column layout -- looks like ordinary spacing to the eye; nothing about it looks wrong until you count the spaces.

Why would a private-use character be hard to spot by eye?

Characters in the Unicode Private Use Area (U+E000-U+F8FF) have no standard glyph. Outside the font that defines them, most editors render them as a small blank box, a question mark, or nothing visible at all -- so a bullet character that displayed as a checkmark icon in your resume software can paste as something that looks like empty space next to your bullet text. Scanning past a line that reads ' Led a team of six' registers as normal; only a tool that checks the character's code point, not its rendered appearance, catches it reliably.

So is doing it by eye pointless?

No -- it is the same underlying technique and it is free. What changes is consistency and what gets checked. A human read is good at noticing the paste is obviously broken or clearly fine; it is not good at counting how many lines have a 4-space mid-line gap, measuring what fraction of the document your email address falls within, or reliably spotting a code point that renders as nothing. This checker runs the same fixed set of checks against the same paste every time, in the browser, with nothing uploaded -- a second pair of eyes that never gets tired of counting spaces.

ATS Resume Checker vs. Jobscan

Two different jobs. Jobscan matches your resume’s wording against one specific job posting, behind an account. This page runs the free, no-account, no-upload copy-paste test for a narrower, earlier question: does the text that comes out of your resume file even extract cleanly, before keywords are worth comparing at all?

What each tool is for

Jobscan is a resume-optimization service built around one core mechanism: you paste in your resume and a target job description, and it scores the overlap between them — hard skills, soft skills, keyword density, and related signals — then tells you which terms from the posting are missing from your resume. That is genuinely useful for tailoring one application to one posting. It runs on an account, has a limited free tier, and a paid plan for scanning more than a handful of applications, based on independent review coverage of the product (Jobscan’s own site was not reachable to confirm current limits or pricing from the session that generated this page, so no dollar figure or scan count is stated here as verified fact).

This checker does a different, earlier job. It needs no job posting and no account. You paste the text copied out of your resume file — the same mechanical extraction an ATS performs — and it flags the specific, documented symptoms of a format that breaks that extraction: icon-font bullet characters that paste as garbage, corrupted text, missing standard section headings, contact info buried where a parser won’t look, missing dates, and signs of a collapsed multi-column layout. It runs free in any browser and nothing you paste is uploaded anywhere.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Does my resume use the right keywords for this specific job posting?Both. Jobscan is the account-based scanner; this page’s step 3 does a simpler free version — paste one posting, see which of its skills and phrases your resume covers and which it never mentions. It is a plain-wording match with a small alias list, with no scoring model behind it, so treat it as a first pass.
Does the text in my resume file even extract cleanly, before keywords matter?This checker — free, instant, private, no account, no posting needed.
Which exact formatting artifact is breaking my resume’s parsing?This checker — each finding names the pattern (icon-font bullets, missing heading, buried contact info) and why it matters.
I want ongoing tailoring across many applications and an account to track them.Jobscan, or a comparable account-based scanner — this checker keeps no history and has no account.
Why does the copy-paste test work as a proxy for ATS parsing?This checker’s own explanation of the technique.
Do I need to sign up or pay to run one check?This checker: no, ever. Jobscan: free tier is limited; unlimited scanning needs a paid plan.

The two are more sequential than rival. A resume with a broken extraction will likely score badly on a keyword match too — not because the wording is wrong, but because the parser never read it correctly to compare it. Running the free format check first, then a keyword tool like Jobscan for a specific posting once the format is clean, gets more out of both.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the checker runs in your browser, and it keeps working with the connection off once loaded.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Jobscan?

They answer different questions, and most job seekers end up wanting both at different points. Jobscan asks: does this resume's wording match the specific job posting I'm applying to? You give it your resume and a job description, it scores hard skills, soft skills and keyword overlap between the two, and tells you which keywords to add. That needs an account, and doing it for more than a handful of applications needs a paid plan. This checker asks a narrower, earlier question: does the text that comes out of my resume file even extract cleanly, before keywords matter at all? You paste text copied out of your resume file -- no job posting needed -- and it flags icon-font bullets, corrupted characters, missing section headings, buried contact info, missing dates, and signs of a collapsed multi-column layout: the structural problems that can make an ATS misread or drop content regardless of which keywords are in it. A resume that fails the format check will likely score badly on a keyword match too, for the wrong reason -- the parser never read the words correctly to compare them. Run the format check first; if it's clean, a keyword tool like Jobscan is the right next step for tailoring to one specific posting.

Does Jobscan check for the same formatting problems this tool does?

Jobscan's own stated mechanism is a match-rate score between your resume and a job description -- hard skills, soft skills, keyword density, and related signals -- and it does also report on some formatting and section-heading issues as part of that scan, according to independent reviews of the product. What this page will not do is describe Jobscan's exact scoring formula, scan limits or current pricing tiers as fact, because Jobscan's own site is not reachable from the session that generated this page and only third-party review coverage was available to check against, which this page treats as informative rather than authoritative. The one difference stated with confidence is the one both tools' own positioning agrees on: Jobscan's central job is matching a resume against a specific job posting's keywords, behind an account; this tool's only job is the format check, with no posting, no account and nothing uploaded.

what-is-the-ats-copy-paste-test.html.text:
ATS RESUME CHECKER

What is the ATS copy-paste test, and why does it work?

An applicant tracking system (ATS) is the software that reads your resume before a person does. Most of them work the same mechanical way: they extract the text from your file — PDF or Word — and parse it into fields like contact info, work history, and skills. They do not "see" your resume the way a human reading a printed page does; they read the underlying text stream, in whatever order the file exposes it.

That is exactly what your operating system's copy command does too. So copying all the text out of your resume file and looking at what comes out is a genuine, if imperfect, simulation of what an ATS parser sees — and it needs no special software, no account, and no upload.

How to run it

  1. Open your resume file (PDF or Word — whatever you actually send to employers).
  2. Select all the text (Ctrl+A / Cmd+A) and copy it (Ctrl+C / Cmd+C).
  3. Paste it somewhere you can actually read it — a plain text editor, or the ATS resume checker on this site, which also flags the specific symptoms below automatically.
  4. Read what came out, not what you remember writing. Is everything there? In the right order? Readable?

What to look for

Garbled or missing characters. If bullet points, checkmarks, or icons turn into odd boxes or unreadable characters, your template is using an icon font for decoration — the character that displays as a bullet in your design software has no meaning outside it, and an ATS reading the raw text sees the same garbage character this test does.

Sections that don't show up at all. If your Skills or Education section is completely missing from the pasted text, that content is probably living in a text box, a graphic, or a table cell that didn't copy as plain text — which usually means it won't extract for an ATS either.

Contact info in the wrong place, or missing. If your name, email, or phone number don't appear near the top — or don't appear at all — check whether they're set in a header or footer. Some ATS platforms deliberately ignore header/footer content because it's inconsistent across resume templates.

Content that reads out of order. Two-column layouts and tables are designed to be read visually, top-to-bottom within each column. A mechanical text extraction usually reads left-to-right per line instead, which can interleave your job titles with your skills list into a scrambled mess.

No dates anywhere. If your employment dates don't show up as plain text (say, because they're in a graphic timeline), an ATS can't build a work-history timeline from them.

What this test can't tell you

It's a proxy, not a guarantee. Different ATS products (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, iCIMS, Taleo, and others) use different parsing engines, and some are considerably more forgiving than others. A resume that copies out cleanly is more likely to parse well broadly, but no free tool — this one included — can promise a specific result on a specific company's system. It also says nothing about whether your resume's content is compelling, relevant to the role, or well-written; that's a separate, and arguably more important, question.

Run the check: back to the ATS resume checker.

No warranty. This page is informational and is not career, legal, or other professional advice. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. Free, experimental, and may change or move without notice.

Free and open source. Support is entirely optional.
